cards.headline: At least 25 injured in car bombing outside government headquarters in Villavicencio, Colombia

pages.text: A car bomb exploded outside the Meta departmental government headquarters in Villavicencio, Colombia, on the night of November 23, 2026. Footage filmed on November 24 shows collapsed building façades, burnt-out vehicles, and streets covered in shattered glass. The blast damaged several homes and businesses, including a shop selling religious images located near the cathedral and parish house. This explosion occurs as Colombia experiences a resurgence of violence driven by rival armed groups competing for control of trafficking networks and illegal economies, particularly near the Venezuelan border.

In Cúcuta, hundreds of residents, police officers, and military personnel held a candlelit march on November 23, 2026. The march was held in solidarity with families affected by a recent attack on the city's police headquarters. According to the regional government, that attack resulted in three people injured, including a child, and caused damage to more than 80 homes.

pages.text: Eleven people were injured after a tower in the financial district of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was targeted in a terrorist Houthi attack, according to Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense. The injured include two Saudi citizens, two residents of Indian nationality, three residents of Nepalese nationality, and four residents of Egyptian nationality. Maj. cards.headline: Ukrainian naval drones sink Russian corvette Merkury in Benghazi, Libya

pages.text: On November 22, 2026, Ukraine deployed naval drones in strikes against two Russian vessels off the coast of Libya, an operation that included the sinking of the Merkury, one of Russia's newest corvettes. The attack took place at the Benghazi naval base, approximately 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine. Residents in Benghazi reported hearing loud explosions and seeing flames at the base early that day, prompting civil defence units to rush to the site to extinguish the fire, according to authorities in eastern Libya. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the mission as an “exemplary operation.” The SBU, Ukraine's security service, stated that seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership during the strike. Zelenskyy also noted that a second vessel, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was hit during the operation and stated the ship was being used by Russia to transport weapons. The Institute for the Study of War reported that the Merkury had stopped in Benghazi for several days to refuel and resupply under a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya while escorting cargo ships that could carry military supplies to Russia. The United Nations mission in Libya has expressed “deep concern” regarding the operation.

cards.headline: UK imposes sanctions on Yemen’s Houthi group and four senior officials

pages.text: The United Kingdom imposed sanctions on Yemen’s Houthi group and four of its senior officials on November 18, 2026, accusing the Iran-backed group of attempting to undermine stability in the Middle East. The measures include asset freezes and travel bans for the sanctioned individuals. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband stated that the group must be held accountable for targeting partners and innocent civilians. The UK government cited Houthi attacks on vessels in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, strikes on civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, and aggression within Yemen as reasons for the action.

The four sanctioned Houthi officials are accused of involvement in human rights abuses. Interior Minister Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi allegedly oversaw the custody of detainees who were subjected to beatings, electric shocks, and sexual violence. Prosecutor Sarim al-Din Muffadal is reasonably suspected of having directly perpetrated, or knowingly permitted or acquiesced in, sexual violence—including rape—and the torture or cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment of women detainees. Also sanctioned are Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani, the security and intelligence chief, and Mohammed Moufleh, a Houthi-appointed judge.

The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, have controlled much of northern and western Yemen since seizing the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014. While a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely halted fighting in 2022, the conflict flared again in July when the group announced a blockade on Saudi ports. The UK government noted that renewed fighting has displaced hundreds of thousands of Yemenis and called for the Houthis to end attacks and allow unimpeded humanitarian access.

cards.headline: Broad Front leader calls for rental sector reform ahead of Spain's snap election

pages.text: Ada Colau, leader of Spain’s left-wing Broad Front coalition, has called for a drastic rethink of the country’s entire housing rental system. In an interview with the Guardian, the former Barcelona mayor stated that her coalition is not interested in small changes but wants to reform the entire sector. Colau expressed hope that public anger over housing issues will translate into support for the Broad Front in the upcoming snap general election. The Broad Front, an alliance founded in February to unite parties to the left of the Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE), named Colau as its candidate for prime minister on 12 October. The alliance does not include the Podemos leftist group or the Catalan Republican Left (ERC) party.

The call for reform follows nationwide protests triggered by the September eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman, from her Madrid apartment. Colau described the eviction as “the last straw” for tenants and said the event “lit the fuse” for the current political situation. The public outrage over Abascal's eviction prompted the government, led by Pedro Sánchez’s PSOE, to propose changes to Spain’s housing laws. However, those proposals were voted down by a combination of right-wing parties and Catalan nationalists, leading Sánchez to call a snap election. Colau, who had stepped out of the political limelight three years ago after failing to win a third term as Barcelona mayor, said she agreed to be a candidate after seeing people take to the streets.

As Spain approaches the election, polls indicate the conservative People’s party (PP) will win the most seats but will fall short of a parliamentary majority. This outcome could allow the far-right Vox party to act as kingmakers. A coalition deal between the PP and Vox would mark the first time the far right has returned to government in Spain's post-dictatorship democratic history.

cards.headline: Emissions in Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area rose 8 per cent from 2024 to 2025

pages.text: Emissions across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) increased by 8 per cent from 2024 to 2025, marking the largest annual jump since tracking began in 2015, according to a report from The Atmospheric Fund. The regional climate agency found that a more polluting energy grid and rising demand for gas heating during a colder winter drove the spike, which represents the fifth consecutive year of rising emissions. This increase puts the region further off track from meeting its climate goals. Bryan Purcell, the agency's vice president of policy and programs, stated the increase brings the region way off track from reaching set climate targets and highlights an urgent need for action to bring emissions back onto a downward trajectory.

Buildings were among the primary drivers of the annual increase, accounting for nearly half of the region's emissions. The GTHA is responsible for a major share of Ontario's emissions and now faces a steep climb to meet local climate commitments. If Toronto's 2030 target were applied as a regional benchmark, emissions would need to be reduced by approximately 16 per cent each year. Purcell noted that the findings challenge the political argument that climate action must be secondary to affordability concerns, suggesting that measures like building retrofits, switching to heat pumps, and improving public transit can also help alleviate financial pressures.

The report identified several recent developments that offer progress toward climate goals, including Toronto removing local barriers to installing electric vehicle chargers and heat pumps, Ontario procuring a record amount of battery storage that beat gas on cost, and a $2-billion federal government investment in building retrofits and heat pump rebates. However, the report stated that government policy rollbacks are threatening to overshadow this progress as climate change fuels more intense heat, flooding, and wildfires. Purcell said that while the technology to move emissions downward exists, the missing ingredient is the political will to implement consistent policies and programs.

cards.headline: Health workers trapped in Ituri province hospital as violence intensifies during DRC Ebola outbreak

pages.text: Staff from the World Health Organization (WHO) and Ebola responders are sheltering in a maternity ward of a hospital in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), due to heavy fighting in the vicinity. The WHO reported that the health workers have been trapped in the ward since fighting began on November 21, 2026, near the area where the current outbreak first emerged in May. This violence comes as personnel attempt to contain the spread of Ebola caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus species. Since January, the WHO has confirmed 87 attacks on healthcare workers and facilities in the DRC. The Africa Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (Africa CDC) noted that the frequency of attacks has increased since the end of October, disrupting hospital work and the wider Ebola response. Richard Hatchett, MD, CEO of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), stated that conflict and misinformation are hindering the large-scale studies needed for the outbreak, noting that the ability to enroll necessary subjects is a dynamic process. Hatchett said three ongoing large vaccine trials could lead to a breakthrough in the beginning of 2027.

The outbreak is placing significant pressure on families, with the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) reporting that women and girls are bearing much of the burden. Fear of the virus has limited their movements, increasing their risk of violence and abuse. UNICEF is conducting what is believed to be the first real-time surveillance of violence against women and adolescent girls during an active disease outbreak. This study is being carried out alongside SOFEPADI, a Congolese women-led organization, and Washington University in the United States. Researchers have spoken to 1,062 women and adolescent girls across five health zones in Ituri province, the epicenter of the outbreak, and are also gathering information from frontline workers and young people via a UNICEF digital platform called U-Report. According to the latest WHO figures, there have been more than 11,613 confirmed cases and 5,678 deaths. As of this weekend, separate figures show 11,793 cases confirmed, including 5,779 deaths, with an overall crude case-fatality rate of 48.9%.

Containment efforts face challenges due to difficulties in identifying contacts early. An Africa CDC report covering May 15 to November 15 found that only 11% of confirmed cases (1,146 of 10,659 with onset from week 19 to week 45) came from contact lists, against a target of 95%. The Africa CDC stated that the response found the other 89% outside those lists, meaning many transmission links were identified too late to monitor contacts. While virus activity peaked in August, national notifications have held at approximately 460 to 480 confirmed cases a week since late September, with the agency stating the outbreak is entering its third month of a plateau. Ituri and Nord Kivu remain the most affected provinces in eastern DRC. A WHO Disease Outbreak News report stated that while Nord Kivu reported the highest number of cases in the last seven days with 235 cases (a 40% increase compared to the previous seven days) as of 17 November, Ituri has remained the most affected province since the outbreak was declared, with 7,946 cumulative confirmed cases and 3,751 deaths, representing a case-fatality rate of 47%.

cards.headline: Gaza health ministry issues epidemic alert following rise in meningitis cases

pages.text: Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert following a sharp increase in meningitis infections, reporting 272 new cases in October. This figure is more than eight times the normal monthly rate of 30 to 50 cases, according to Dr. Nidal Ghoneim, a senior official at the ministry. Dr. Ghoneim stated at a news conference that the spread of the disease poses a threat to the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, including children. Since the beginning of the conflict, 15 Palestinians have died of meningitis, Dr. Ghoneim said. The health ministry stated it holds the Israeli occupation fully and directly responsible for the outbreak, citing the prevention of entry for fuel, sterilization materials, and maintenance spare parts.

The United Nations humanitarian agency (Ocha) previously reported 413 suspected cases of meningitis in Gaza between 27 September and 31 October, consisting of 294 viral and 119 bacterial cases. Approximately 68% of these suspected cases were recorded in Gaza City. Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to overcrowded shelters, destroyed infrastructure, and the contamination of drinking water with sewage. Ocha noted that the increase could be linked to exposure to unsafe water and the deterioration of sanitation conditions in crowded schools and tents, a situation exacerbated by restrictions on humanitarian aid and winter flooding.

Gaza faces a severe water crisis. Before the war, 80% of the territory’s water supply came from an aquifer that is now unfit for human consumption due to contamination by wastewater and seawater. Much of the territory's drinking water previously relied on desalination plants and three pipelines controlled by Israel; these were cut off at the start of the war and have only partially reopened.

cards.headline: England records 5,258 heat-associated deaths during 2026 summer

pages.text: England recorded 5,258 deaths associated with extreme heat between May and September 2026, according to a provisional report from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA). This figure is the highest annual total since the agency began monitoring heat-related mortality in 2016. The 2026 total is substantially higher than the previous record of 2,985 deaths recorded in 2022. Previous annual totals included 2,295 deaths in 2023, 1,311 in 2024, and 1,504 in another year. The summer was the hottest on record, characterized by record-breaking temperatures and prolonged dry weather, including England's driest July on record with just 7mm of rain.

The highest number of deaths occurred during a heatwave between 21 and 28 June, when an estimated 2,401 people died. More than 3,000 heat-associated deaths were recorded across the first two episodes of the season in May and June. The summer included seven heat episodes lasting a total of 41 days, which is the highest number of episodes and heat-episode days since monitoring began in 2016. During the June heatwave, temperatures reached 38C (100.4F) in Norfolk, and the period triggered only the second red heat-health alert ever issued in England. In August, a peak temperature of 38.2C was recorded in Gloucestershire.

Dr. Ross Thompson, the UKHSA’s principal environmental health scientist, stated that climate change is already affecting health in England and that extreme heat periods are expected to become longer, more frequent, and more intense as the climate warms. Thompson noted that decisions made now regarding the preparedness of individuals, communities, and health services will shape future health impacts. This mortality data follows a period where researchers from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine estimated more than 50,000 heat-related deaths occurred in urban areas across 30 European countries during the summer, the highest toll recorded since 2000.

cards.headline: Banned Awami League and affiliates held 72 flash processions in November, official says

pages.text: The activities-banned Awami League and its affiliated organizations—the Krishak League, Jubo League, and Chhatra League—organized 72 flash processions during the first 23 days of November, according to Zahed Ur Rahman, the Prime Minister's Information and Broadcasting Advisor. Speaking at a press conference at the Secretariat on November 24, 2026, Ur Rahman stated that because there is a legal ban on the activities of the party, these processions are illegal and will result in further cases and arrests. The statistics were compiled using information from the Ministry of Home Affairs and the police. Regarding the 72 processions, 22 cases and 5 general diaries (GD) have been filed, and 66 people have been arrested.

During the same 23-day period in November, 121 incidents of cocktail or bomb explosions occurred in various parts of Bangladesh. These violent incidents resulted in one death and 11 injuries. Authorities reported that 62 cases and 27 general diaries (GD) were filed in connection with the explosions, and 100 people were arrested. Additionally, there were 99 incidents of setting fire to vehicles and four attacks on police establishments during this period.

cards.headline: Malaysia to deport thousands of migrants and refugees to Myanmar

pages.text: Malaysia will send thousands of migrants and refugees back to Myanmar, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced, despite acknowledging that many asylum seekers in the country were victims of “atrocities” committed by the Myanmar regime. The decision follows a ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ)—the United Nations' highest court—which found that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya minority. While the exact number of Rohingya among those facing deportation is unclear, the UN reports that the Rohingya, a Muslim minority group, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers currently in Malaysia. Many Rohingya fled to Malaysia during a military crackdown in 2017.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim stated that the deportations align with advice from the ICJ to “guarantee a safe and dignified return” for those fleeing persecution. He maintained that Malaysia has not abandoned its principles regarding the rights of the people of Myanmar, but argued the country can no longer afford to host refugees and that efforts to resettle them in third countries had not worked. The UN has previously warned that migrants returned to Myanmar could face a dangerous homecoming. Within Malaysia, some people have expressed increasing frustration with the presence of refugees, citing financial burdens, security risks, and a rise in anti-migrant sentiment.

cards.headline: National mortgage delinquency rate in Canada rises 31.1 per cent in third quarter

pages.text: The national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate in Canada reached 0.32 per cent in the third quarter, the highest level since Equifax Canada began tracking the metric in 2013. This rate, which defines a delinquency as missed payments for three consecutive months, represents a 31.1 per cent increase year-over-year. According to Equifax Canada's third-quarter consumer credit trends report, the rise was mainly driven by missed mortgage payments in Ontario and British Columbia. Rebecca Oakes, Equifax Canada's vice-president of advanced analytics, stated that the rate is still going up and is particularly high for Ontario.

The increase in delinquencies follows the Bank of Canada raising its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent. This rate hike prompted major banks to raise their prime rates, which are used to set interest rates for various loans, including variable-rate mortgages. Equifax estimates that approximately 1.4 million Canadians hold a variable-rate mortgage out of a total of 9.1 million homeowners. The company also estimates that every quarter-point rate hike adds roughly $860 million a year in interest on variable-rate mortgages. Additionally, 1.3 million consumers have a home equity line of credit balance of more than $50,000.

Data from Equifax aligns with a recent report from TD, where economist Maria Solovieva noted that elevated mortgage balances and greater sensitivity to borrowing costs are contributing to the trend. The TD report showed that mortgage arrears in Ontario have nearly tripled from pre-pandemic levels, approaching the peak seen during the 2008 financial crisis. Rebecca Oakes suspects that mortgage delinquencies will continue to rise in the coming months, depending on changes to interest rates.

cards.headline: South Korean residents ordered to take shelter after Russian military aircraft approach Ulleungdo

pages.text: Residents of Ulleungdo, a volcanic island of approximately 8,700 people located 120km off the east coast of South Korea, were ordered to take shelter after several Russian military aircraft approached the island's airspace. The South Korean interior ministry issued an emergency alert at 7:52 a.m. containing the English message “EVACUATION, AIR RAID.” Television broadcasts were interrupted with warnings for residents to prepare to evacuate to nearby underground shelter facilities and listen to broadcasting. The alert was lifted at 7:55 a.m. (or 7:58 a.m., according to provincial authorities). During the alert, sirens sounded on the island and residents reported hearing the noise of fighter jets. Jeong Hae-seung, a 41-year-old worker on a building site, told the Hankyoreh newspaper that he ran out of his workplace the moment the text arrived.

The South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) stated that the aircraft entered the country’s air defense identification zone (ADIZ)—a buffer area where countries monitor flight activity to protect sovereign airspace—over the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan. JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the aircraft approached “to the point just before violating Ulleungdo’s airspace” and that a violation was anticipated because military aircraft move very fast. The military scrambled South Korean air force jets before the aircraft left. While the JCS did not specify the number of Russian aircraft involved, the defense ministry later clarified that the planes entered the ADIZ without prior notification and flew in close proximity to the airspace near Ulleungdo. The defense ministry stated the alerts were issued as a precautionary measure to protect residents.

South Korean authorities initially issued an alert suggesting a suspected North Korean aircraft had made an incursion, but later corrected this, stating it was Russian aircraft. Provincial authorities issued a correction approximately 40 minutes after the initial warning, and the defense ministry released a statement clarifying that reports of a North Korean aircraft violating airspace were not true. In response to the incident, Kim Hak-jo, the defense ministry’s director general for international policy, summoned the Russian defense attaché, Colonel Nikolai Marchenko, to lodge a strong protest. The ministry urged Moscow to take measures to prevent a recurrence, describing the repeated incidents as “unacceptable.”

cards.headline: Iraq orders federal takeover of oilfields in Kurdish-controlled areas

pages.text: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the federal Ministry of Oil to manage oilfields located in areas under the security control of the Kurdistan region. The order covers oilfields in the Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin, and Nineveh provinces, according to a statement from the prime minister's office. Under the directive, Baghdad intends to secure and monitor these fields using cameras, including those within federal administrative boundaries that currently fall under the security authority of the regional government. This move follows an inquiry into oil smuggling and may increase disputes between the national government and the semi-autonomous northern region regarding oil control and the sharing of budgetary resources.

In addition to the oilfield directive, Prime Minister al-Zaidi ordered the border crossings authority to take over all crossings in the Kurdish region. The Border Forces Command has been instructed to close unofficial crossings along international borders with neighboring countries, including those in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, and to close all seasonal roads between the four specified governorates and the Kurdish region. Furthermore, the prime minister directed the regional government to approve exports of crude oil and petroleum products only through the federal Oil Ministry. Masoud Barzani, president of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and former president of the Kurdistan region, called the decision “troubling.” Barzani stated the move attempts to undermine the Iraqi constitution and the principles of federalism while disregarding the rights of the people of Kurdistan. While Barzani noted the KDP's willingness to cooperate with the government to prevent smuggling, he maintained such actions must occur through legal and constitutional channels.

cards.headline: India pledges $1.62bn economic package to Nepal for flood reconstruction

pages.text: India has announced a 240 billion Nepali rupee ($1.62bn) development cooperation package to assist Nepal in recovering from devastating floods that occurred in August. The announcement followed talks in New Delhi between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah during Shah's first bilateral trip abroad since taking office in March. The package includes a $377m grant for new infrastructure projects and post-disaster reconstruction, alongside a $1.24bn line of credit for energy projects, according to a joint statement from both countries. This commitment is one of India's largest-ever relief efforts and comes as New Delhi competes with China for influence in its Himalayan neighbor. India is currently Nepal's largest trading partner, accounting for more than 60 percent of its $8.6bn in imports, while China accounts for 13 percent, or $1.8bn, according to World Bank figures.

The August 26 floods were triggered when a mountain glacier collapsed, sending a torrent of water and mud into Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot regions and into China’s Tibet region. Scientists stated the disaster, which they attributed to the effects of climate change, involved the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier. The resulting rockfall registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event. The surge of water and debris swept away homes, buildings, roads, and bridges. Regarding the human toll, Al Jazeera reports that more than 1,300 people have been confirmed dead and more than 5,000 remain missing, while Euronews reports more than 1,400 people were killed and 5,000 left missing. Additionally, at least 900 workers were reported missing from 12 hydropower projects damaged by the floods.

The Indian aid package follows other international relief efforts, including $20m set aside in October by the United Nations’ climate loss and damage fund for aid to Nepal. Nepal estimates the total cost of reconstruction at €4.35 billion. Beyond the flood relief, Prime Minister Modi and Prime Minister Shah agreed to further cooperation in satellite communications, education and research, and sustainable urban development. Shah stated the disaster demonstrated the necessity of addressing climate change challenges through collective action.

cards.headline: Israel seeks administrative detention for Palestinian student activist Mahdi Tounsi

pages.text: Israeli authorities are seeking to hold Mahdi Tounsi, a 26-year-old sociology and criminology student at Hebrew University in Jerusalem, in administrative detention without trial. Administrative detention is a practice where a person is held by the state without formal charges or a trial. This follows the expiration of the original arrest warrant for Tounsi, an East Jerusalem resident, after police seized him from his dorm room on 8 November. The order for his detention was signed by Defence Minister Israel Katz.

Tounsi has been held without charge for more than two weeks. During a court hearing via video link on 19 November, he appeared with visible facial bruising, lacked the glasses he requires to see properly, and had his hair and beard shaved. Tounsi told his lawyer that police beat him in his dorm, in a patrol car, and at a police station, according to reports in Israeli media. Interrogators questioned him regarding his activism with the Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups Standing Together and Ir Amim.

Israeli professors, students, and rights activists are calling for Tounsi's immediate release. Both Standing Together and Ir Amim issued statements calling for his release and warning against the use of security agencies to silence political speech. Ir Amim expressed concerns for Tounsi's safety, wellbeing, and right to due process, describing him as a partner in movements that bring Palestinians and Israelis together. Standing Together urged Hebrew University to intervene to ensure a fair judicial process, stating that such actions could happen to any student.

cards.headline: Syrian migrants accuse UK-based man of organizing deadly Libya crossing

pages.text: Three Syrian migrants have accused a Syrian man based in the United Kingdom of arranging journeys to Europe that resulted in detention, alleged abuse, and a deadly Mediterranean crossing. An investigation by Syria Direct identified the man accused of arranging the voyage for one of the migrants, an engineering student identified as Sameer*.

Sameer* reported that the UK-based fixer promised safe passage and claimed the crossing was more than guaranteed and dependable. To fund the journey, Sameer* and his family sold possessions from his deceased father, including his car, raising $13,000. His journey began in autumn 2025, during which he experienced detention and abuse and witnessed the deaths of fellow migrants. While some of his fellow migrants remain missing, stranded, or detained, Sameer* survived.

cards.headline: Indigenous women plant native Kewiña trees to restore water sources in the Bolivian Andes

pages.text: Indigenous women in the Tunari mountain range of Bolivia’s central Cochabamba department are planting native Kewiña trees to combat chronic drought and increasing erosion. The Kewiña (Polylepis sp.) is a slow-growing tree belonging to the rose family that can thrive at high elevations up to approximately 4,450 meters (14,600 feet) above sea level. These trees provide critical ecosystem services for the Cochabamba metropolitan area and the nearby Amazon basin, while also serving as a vital habitat for the near threatened Cochabamba mountain finch (Poospiza garleppi). As of November 24, 2026, the region's landscape is characterized by bare ridges, occasional shrubby trees, and potato crops, reflecting a significant loss of original vegetation.

Biologists estimate that only 10% of the region’s original Kewiña tree coverage remains. This decline is attributed to decades of clearing for firewood, construction, and small-scale potato agriculture, alongside urban expansion, intensifying wildfires, and habitat fragmentation. Additionally, the area has experienced drier and warmer weather linked to forest loss and climate change. In 2023, the IUCN listed one Polylepis species endemic to central Bolivia as endangered. Andrea Vicente, a potato farmer in the village of Chiaraje—located at approximately 3,780 meters (12,400 feet) in the Tunari mountains—noted that residents previously harvested firewood from the Kewiña without replanting. Tunari National Park, which covers about 309,000 hectares (763,500 acres), contains a large but much reduced population of these trees.

cards.headline: Akashmoni plantations are replacing Sal trees in Bangladesh's Bhawal forest

pages.text: Large stretches of the Bhawal Sal forest in Bangladesh are being replaced by Akashmoni (Acacia auriculiformis) plantations, according to a report by The Business Standard. While the forest appears lush and green from the Dhaka–Mymensingh highway, the canopy hides the fact that much of the area is no longer composed of Sal trees. Instead, neatly trimmed and well-groomed Akashmoni trees occupy areas where the Sal woodland ends abruptly. In some sections, a thin layer of Sal trees serves to shield the Acacia plantations from the view of travelers on the highway.

cards.headline: Biologists discover a bright yellow burbot in Oswego Harbor, New York

pages.text: Biologists from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) discovered a vibrantly colored burbot during a routine invasive species survey in Oswego Harbor, New York. The fish, which the USFWS described as “one-in-a-million,” possesses an unusually saturated yellow hue that contrasts with the mottled olive green, earthy brown, and golden yellow colors typical of the species. While burbots are native to the Great Lakes, they generally inhabit cooler, deeper waters than those found in Oswego Harbor on Lake Ontario. According to a November 10 announcement, the fish was in rough shape despite its striking color.

The burbot's appearance is due to xanthochromism, a rare biological condition caused by a genetic mutation. This mutation reduces the production of black-brown melanin, a pigment that normally colors animals, allowing yellow pigment to dominate and produce an unusually saturated yellow or orange hue. In wild fish, the USFWS notes that xanthochromism is much less common than albinism, which causes pale or white coloring, or melanism, which produces unusually dark coloring. While xanthochromism has been observed in dozens of fish species as well as birds and amphibians, it has only been recorded in a handful of mammals, including anteaters, tayras, opossums, pikas, martens, weasels, and coatis.

cards.headline: Displaced families in Damascus fight for justice over Marota City redevelopment projects

pages.text: Families displaced by redevelopment projects in Damascus, Syria, are seeking justice as the current administration maintains the vision for the area's transformation. The Marota City and Basilia City projects, covering approximately 2,200 acres, were established by Legislative Decree No. 66, issued in 2012 by then-President Bashar al-Assad. The decree allowed for the expropriation of land to make way for modern urban development. Under this law, expropriated landowners were to receive shares that could be sold or pooled with others to obtain plots in future towers, though developing these plots required partnering with other owners and covering construction costs. Residents were also entitled to alternative housing or rental allowances, but many claim they received neither the promised housing nor adequate compensation. By 2017, the project had displaced around 7,500 families. The targeted area, spanning parts of al-Mazzeh and Basatin al-Razi, was a politically sensitive, affluent neighborhood located near the presidential palace, diplomatic missions, a United Nations office, and Daraya, a center of opposition to the former regime. Mohammad al-Moallem, a resident in his 50s whose property was expropriated, alleged that authorities labeled the neighborhood a slum and a threat to justify displacement, claiming the area was viewed as harboring sleeper cells of the revolution. Despite the fall of the Assad regime, the vision for the area remains consistent. Ghiyath al-Idlibi, the head of investments at the Damascus Governorate offices under the administration led by interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa, stated that the goal is to create a 'Dubai-style city' featuring skyscrapers ranging from 13 to 70 floors, gardens, and a tower intended as a headquarters for tech companies. Al-Idlibi said the vision remains the same as before the fall of Assad, but aims to be better by widening streets.

cards.headline: 112 Bangladeshi workers scheduled for zero-cost flight to Malaysia

pages.text: A group of 112 Bangladeshi workers is scheduled to depart Dhaka for Kuala Lumpur on November 26, 2026, marking a reopening of Malaysia's labour market for Bangladesh after more than two years. The workers will travel on a commercial Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight departing Shahjalal International Airport at 7pm following an inauguration by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. This flight is a zero-cost departure, as the employer, DHL Supply Chain Malaysia, is covering all travel costs for the workers. This initiative is part of a first-phase drive to send 10,000 workers to Malaysia.

The workers were recruited through the Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), a state agency. BOESL Managing Director Mohammad Rashedul Haque stated that the selection process involved an automated lottery from 4,029 applicants, followed by practical and oral tests to ensure neutrality and transparency. This recruitment follows a period during which Malaysia halted the hiring of Bangladeshi workers in June 2024, citing corruption, excessive fees, and syndicate irregularities. Prior to that halt, between 2022 and May 2024, Malaysia hired approximately 450,000 Bangladeshi workers.

cards.headline: An estimated 1.2 lakh children work in Keraniganj’s informal garment sector

pages.text: An estimated 1.2 lakh children work in the informal ready-made garment (RMG) sector in Keraniganj, Bangladesh, according to the Bangladesh Labour Foundation (BLF). Of the approximately 2.5 lakh workers employed across some 7,500 production units in the area, the BLF reported that around 20,000 of these children are aged below 14. These figures were shared on November 23, 2026, during a launch event for a joint project between the BLF and the International Labour Organization (ILO) aimed at reducing child labour. Speaking at the event, Dr. Mahdi Amin, adviser to the prime minister and PMO spokesperson, stated that children should be in classrooms rather than factories. He noted that the government intends to expand social protection and educational support through a National Plan of Action for 2026-30 to address the issue.

The joint BLF and ILO project, supported by the ILO’s ADWIB programme under the Team Europe Initiative, is scheduled to run from October 2026 to September 2027. The initiative targets 4,500 children in the Aganagar and Suvadda unions of Keraniganj, including 900 children aged below 14. During the launch in Dhaka, EU Delegation representative Michal Krejza warned that child labour could affect Bangladesh’s international image, investment, and trade. Other speakers at the event included BLF Executive Director AKM Ashraf Uddin, Socialist Labour Front President Rajekuzzaman Ratan, and Md Abdur Rahim Khan, an additional secretary of the labour ministry.

cards.headline: Female bottlenose dolphins change social positions based on fertility status

pages.text: A study published in Animal Behaviour suggests that female common bottlenose dolphins may alter their social circles depending on whether they are reproductively active, pregnant, or nursing. Researchers analyzing more than a decade of data from 1,253 wild dolphin sightings in Spain found that a female's social network shifts according to her reproductive stage. Bruno Díaz López, director at the Bottlenose Dolphin Research Institute (BRDI) and author of the study, noted that lactating females tend to maintain stronger and more selective relationships with specific individuals, while females in their reproductive cycle occupy more central positions within the social network.

The researchers categorized the ``cycling state'' as the six-month period preceding conception, a phase when females are most likely to engage in social interactions related to mating. According to Díaz López, females in this cycling state act as ``social butterflies,'' meeting new individuals and maintaining connections with well-connected members of the community. The study suggests this high level of social integration may be a strategy to maximize mating opportunities. In contrast, when a dolphin becomes pregnant and is no longer mating, she remains integrated within the group but pulls back slightly from some social interactions.

cards.headline: Ontario nurses report extreme burnout and moral injury in new report

pages.text: A report released on November 23, 2026, by the Ontario Council of Hospital Unions (OCHU)—the hospital division of the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE)—details accounts of stress and burnout among nurses in Ontario hospitals. The report, co-authored by University of Windsor sociology adjunct professors James Brophy and Margaret Keith, contains interviews and testimonies from 14 Ontario hospital nurses describing hospitals they say are understaffed and under-resourced. James Brophy stated the nurses are describing a level of burnout and moral injury that has become the new norm, suggesting the issue is reaching a tipping point. Moral injury refers to mental distress caused by the inability to provide patients with necessary care.

Nurses interviewed in the report described various workplace challenges, including inadequate equipment and increased violence. A nurse using the pseudonym Sumaia reported not having working equipment or computers to perform her job. Another nurse, referred to as Kim, said she had seen an increase in violence against health-care staff and witnessed a nurse knocked unconscious by an ER patient. One medical-surgical nurse, using the pseudonym Jane, described a chaotic shift where she attempted to split her attention among five high-need patients. Jane stated that when she asked for help, other staff members were also overwhelmed with their own patients. During that shift, a palliative care patient died, leaving Jane with fears regarding whether she would be conscious for the patient's last breath or face legal action for leaving a patient unattended in a washroom.

cards.headline: Euclid space telescope discovers most distant quasar seen 630 million years after Big Bang

pages.text: The European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope has identified a rare galactic core with a mass of 360 million suns, seen just 630 million years after the Big Bang. This discovery, of the object formally known as J1504+6252 and nicknamed Dún Aonghasa, breaks Euclid’s own previous record by peering back in time an additional 40 million years. The object was identified among millions of items within approximately 18 months of Euclid data. This finding raises questions regarding how such an enormous black hole could have formed and grown so rapidly following the Big Bang. A quasar is an intensely bright galaxy core powered by gas falling into a supermassive black hole, a process that releases enormous amounts of energy. Quasars represent a brief phase in a galaxy’s life where the nucleus can outshine the rest of the system. The nature of J1504+6252 was confirmed through a follow-up campaign by ground- and space-based observatories, including the W.M. Keck Observatory, the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory, the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope, and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope.

cards.headline: More than 310 million-year-old fossil reveals scorpion similar to modern species

pages.text: A small fossil scorpion discovered in a North American coal deposit lived more than 310 million years ago during the Carboniferous period. Researchers from Flinders University, the University of Alabama, and the American Museum of Natural History in the U.S. found that the specimen is remarkably similar in physical form to modern scorpions. The research, published in The Science of Nature, provides new insights into the evolution of these nocturnal, venomous arthropods. Because of its relatively small size, researchers suspect the fossil could be a juvenile specimen. They also noted that it may be one of the first of its kind to be examined and connected to the evolution of modern scorpions on the North American continent.

While the fossil closely resembles modern relatives, researchers noted it might not be completely within the modern scorpion group because one pair of eyes is slightly too far forward. Modern scorpions typically possess between six and 12 eyes, consisting of an obvious pair at the center of the carapace and two to five smaller eyes on each side, though they generally do not have good eyesight. Their distinctive shape includes a long, sting-bearing tail and a pair of pincers on long arms, known as pedipalps, located at the front of the body.

cards.headline: Isotope analysis suggests people traveled long distances to Colchester, Roman Britain's first capital

pages.text: Analysis of strontium and lead isotopes in 2,000-year-old cremated remains indicates that several of 22 individuals buried in Colchester, the first capital of Roman Britannia, grew up thousands of miles away. Researchers from Durham University developed a method to analyze these isotopes in remains that had been subjected to the intense heat of funeral pyres, which typically makes such analysis difficult. This finding suggests a diverse population in the region during the Roman period.

One example includes cremated remains found buried in the Colchester Vase, a container decorated with scenes of animal hunting and gladiatorial combat. Analysis showed this individual grew up in the Mediterranean region. Based on the imagery on the vessel, researchers suggest this person may have been a patron who funded gladiator fights or may have trained gladiators. The study, conducted by Joanna Moore, Janet Montgomery, Geoff Nowell, and colleagues from Durham University, was published in Royal Society Open Science.

cards.headline: Bronze neck ring from 2000 to 1700 B.C. discovered in Swiss Alps

pages.text: Retreating ice in the Lötschen Pass, a mountain pass in the eastern Bernese Alps, has revealed a rigid bronze neck ring featuring small loops at its ends. Researchers from the Archaeological Service of the Canton of Bern dated the jewelry to between 2000 and 1700 B.C. The artifact was found at an elevation of more than 8,500 feet above sea level. Researchers believe the neckwear may have been left in the mountains as an offering to a deity.

The discovery suggests regular movement through Alpine passes approximately 4,000 years ago. Researchers explained that similar neck rings have been found in graves on the other side of the Bernese Alps on the shore of Lake Thun.

cards.headline: Scientists observe vaporized titanium oxide around young star in Orion

pages.text: Researchers have observed titanium oxide in gas form around a massive, young star for the first time. Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, the team studied the disk of Orion Source I, a massive, young star located in a dusty cloud behind the Orion Nebula. This discovery allows scientists to determine the composition of solid materials outside of our solar system without needing to collect and return physical samples to Earth. Previously, mineralogists could examine rocks on Earth, but there was no way to study the makeup of rocky objects in space. By observing vaporized rock, researchers can now understand what solid objects in space are made of through remote observation.

University of Florida Associate Professor of Astronomy Adam Ginsburg, Ph.D., identified the system examined by the research team and developed some of the techniques used to analyze it. Ginsburg noted that while scientists typically evaporate material in a laboratory to measure its composition using a spectrograph, this discovery provides a way to observe similar processes occurring naturally in the interstellar medium. The finding marks the first region where scientists have been able to determine the composition of solid materials outside our solar system in this manner.
